question: Which of the following congenital heart defects produces cyanosis at presentation in adults?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An uncomplicated ASD produces a left-to-right shunt (acyanotic). Cyanosis only develops if Eisenmenger syndrome supervenes (right-to-left shunt reversal due to pulmonary hypertension). ASD is the most common cause of Eisenmenger syndrome in adults, but the defect itself is initially acyanotic.

PDA produces a left-to-right shunt (acyanotic). Again, Eisenmenger physiology can cause differential cyanosis (cyanosis of the lower limbs/toes but not the upper limbs/fingers), but the native PDA is an acyanotic lesion.

Correct. Tetralogy of Fallot (VSD + overriding aorta + right ventricular hypertrophy + right ventricular outflow tract obstruction) causes a right-to-left shunt at the VSD level, resulting in cyanosis from birth/infancy. Adults with repaired ToF may present with residual pulmonary regurgitation or VSD, but ToF is the archetypal cyanotic congenital defect.
A small isolated VSD produces a left-to-right shunt and is acyanotic. It may close spontaneously. Cyanosis only occurs if Eisenmenger physiology develops in a large unrepaired VSD.

overallFeedback.feedback: The fundamental division: acyanotic CHD = left-to-right shunts (ASD, VSD, PDA, AVSD). Cyanotic CHD = right-to-left or mixed shunts (ToF, TGA, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia). ToF is the classic cyanotic lesion.
Correct. Tetralogy of Fallot is the classic cyanotic CHD producing right-to-left shunting. ASD, VSD, and PDA are acyanotic (left-to-right) unless complicated by Eisenmenger syndrome.
